content: 1. Gatifloxacin, when used as ZYMAXID® solution, is strictly for topical ophthalmic use and must not be introduced directly into the anterior chamber of the eye. 2. The use of ZYMAXID® solution at a concentration of 0.5% may lead to the overgrowth of organisms that are not susceptible to the drug, including fungi. 3. If a superinfection occurs during treatment, the use of ZYMAXID® should be discontinued, and an alternative therapy should be initiated. 4. Patients should be examined with magnification tools, such as slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and fluorescein staining should be used when clinically indicated to assess the condition of the eye. 5. Patients should be advised to avoid wearing contact lenses if they exhibit signs or symptoms of bacterial conjunctivitis or during the course of therapy with ZYMAXID®. 6. ZYMAXID® is classified as Pregnancy Category C. No teratogenic effects were observed in rats or rabbits at oral doses up to 50 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 1000 times higher than the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose. 7. However, skeletal and craniofacial malformations, delayed ossification, atrial enlargement, and reduced fetal weight were observed in rat fetuses at doses of 150 mg/kg/day or higher, which is approximately 3000 times the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose. 8. In perinatal and postnatal studies, increased late post-implantation loss and neonatal/perinatal mortality were observed at doses of 200 mg/kg/day, approximately 4000 times the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose. 9. Due to the lack of adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, ZYMAXID® should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 10. Gatifloxacin is excreted in the breast milk of rats, but it is unknown whether it is excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised when administering ZYMAXID® to nursing women, as many drugs are excreted in human milk. 11. The safety and effectiveness of ZYMAXID® in infants under one year of age have not been established. However, clinical trials have demonstrated its safety and efficacy in treating bacterial conjunctivitis in pediatric patients aged one year and older. 12. No significant differences in safety or effectiveness have been observed between elderly and younger patients when using ZYMAXID®. 13. Long-term carcinogenicity studies in B6C3F1 mice and Fischer 344 rats showed no increase in neoplasms at dietary doses of gatifloxacin up to 81 mg/kg/day in male mice, 90 mg/kg/day in female mice, 47 mg/kg/day in male rats, and 139 mg/kg/day in female rats. These doses are significantly higher (900-2800 times) than the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose. 14. A statistically significant increase in large granular lymphocyte (LGL) leukemia was observed in male rats treated with a high dose of gatifloxacin, approximately 2000 times the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose. However, this finding slightly exceeded the historical control range for this strain, which has a high spontaneous background rate of LGL leukemia. 15. In genetic toxicity tests, gatifloxacin was positive in one of five strains used in bacterial reverse mutation assays (Salmonella strain TA102). It was also positive in in vitro mammalian cell mutation and chromosome aberration assays. 16. Gatifloxacin was positive in in vitro unscheduled DNA synthesis in rat hepatocytes but not in human leukocytes. 17. Gatifloxacin was negative in in vivo micronucleus tests in mice, cytogenetics tests in rats, and DNA repair tests in rats. 18. The observed findings may be attributed to the inhibitory effects of high concentrations of gatifloxacin on eukaryotic type II DNA topoisomerase.
